Portfolio optimization is a critical application in Finance, yet its computational intricacies compel financial institutions to resort to simplified methods that require considerable time. By leveraging the Lagrange multiplier method, the mean-variance portfolio optimization issue can be formulated into a set of linear equations and potentially take advantage of the accelerated performance offered by the HHL quantum algorithm. Nevertheless, certain HHL components are not well-suited for operation on Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum hardware. This research introduces NISQ-HHL, the first hybrid rendition of HHL that is capable of supporting end-to-end execution of compact-scale portfolio-optimization tasks on NISQ devices. NISQ-HHL enhances the hybrid HHL variation with newly available quantum-hardware capabilities, encompassing mid-circuit measurement, qubit reinitialization and quantum reinitialization and quantum-algorithms made feasible by these capabilities. Moreover, NISQ-HHL incorporates an innovative application of quantum hardware that utilizes quantum expression compilers to convert classical expression files into executable code. This research also presents an extended quantum-hardware-compatible execution of the quantum phase estimation algorithm. Numerical simulations demonstrate that NISQ-HHL's performance outshines both classical and other hybrid HHL-rendering algorithms in terms of precision and computational efficiency. NISQ-HHL's final product exhibits a higher degree of accuracy and computational efficiency.

To enhance data efficiency of state-of-the-art end-to-end ASR models and enable them to handle a large amount of unpaired text data through multi-modal training, it's essential that they capture the alignment between speech and corresponding text. However, many things we've so far tried fail to effectively represent the true attention mechanism between the two. In order to address this, this paper proposes a bidirectional attention mechanism that reflects true text-to-speech and speech-to-text relationships, which uses two components: a mutual attention module and a text-to-text learning algorithm with bibtex. As a result, this mechanism allows us to skip module components for end-to-end ASR, but provides significant performance gains when added, and in doing so it enables learning from unpaired text data. Experimental data shows a 5.3% reduction in word error rate on the LibriSpeech corpus, which translates to an 11.5% improvement. This module component also yields a 8.7% reduction in word error rate when trained on the weakly paired text data.

This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly selected uniform parking function from $n$ functions with length $n$, focusing on the first non-zero and last zero positions. As the function's length approaches infinity, we find that the asymptotic distribution of these positions can be modeled by a Poisson process with an inter-arrival time distribution of uniform spacings. Furthermore, we establish precise relationships and limit theorems, including $r_n-s_n\approx\sqrt{n}$ and $\frac{r_n+s_n}{2}\approx\frac{2n}{3}\frac{\Gamma(\frac{2}{3})}{\Gamma(\frac{1}{3})}$. Our research also extends to parking functions of varying lengths and provides insights into combinatorial sequences found in the On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences.

Measurements of superconducting nanowires, particularly NbN nanowires, indicate the presence of a critical voltage threshold for dc conduction below which coherent quantum phase slips dominate, potentially blocking conduction. The critical voltage of these nanowires is observed to be sensitive to the application of an external magnetic field perpendicular to the nanowire, in direct contrast to the expected insensitivity to such a field. The application of a longitudinal magnetic field is seen to modify critical voltage in accordance with effective length modifications, whereas a perpendicular field is observed to alter critical voltage, again contradicting prior expectations. The alteration of critical voltage by a perpendicular field is interpreted as implying that grain boundaries of the nanowire are in effect acting as Josephson junctions. The research is further extended to Meissner effect observations, where nanowires exhibit localized supercurrents that oppose the applied field, confirming that critical voltages are influenced by grain boundaries and located at the nanowire ends.

Our proposed approach tackles the challenge of novel view video prediction, taking input from multiple viewpoints. Unlike existing research that relies on narrow angle variations, our network can generate videos from significantly wider angles, up to 45 degrees, without the need for prior knowledge. By processing only RGB frames, we've developed a two-component representation, combining local and global features that enables novel view prediction. Our model achieves remarkable results on real-world datasets NTU-RGB+D and CMU Panoptic, surpassing the state-of-the-art in novel view video prediction, demonstrating significant gains in SSIM, PSNR, and FVD scores of 26.1%, 13.6%, and 60% respectively, without the use of prior views.

In this research, inter-orbital coupling was demonstrated using femtosecond laser writing, which enables orthogonal modes in a photonic lattice to couple with each other at different spatial locations. We characterized an asymmetric double-well structure, mapped its propagation dynamics and successfully created a device capable of spatial mode conversion anywhere within a photonic chip. Utilizing higher-order photonic mode phase structure, our experiment showed that a trimer configuration can serve as a $\pi$-phase beam splitter for multiplexing and other interference-based photonic applications.

The Ω-baryon, which contains sss quarks and has only been marginally detected in past experiments, has primarily been studied using theoretical methods so far. A study aims to explore this particle's properties utilizing a quark model with linear confining forces. Calculated resonance masses are presented for the ground and excited states of S, P, D, and F quark systems. A linear nature of the Regge trajectory, supported by calculated data and magnetic moments, has also been examined. This study compares its results to other approaches and available experimental evidence.

Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay between turbulent airflow, respiration processes, coughing, and sneezing, as well as various ventilation methods, temperature-driven buoyancy effects, and surface deposition of aerosols. To better understand and quantify this complex dynamic, we used numerical models of unsteady airflow to analyze and visualize virus-laden aerosol transport. In comparing our detailed model to a widely accepted 'well mixed' model, notable discrepancies in the distribution of aerosol particles became evident, with implications for our understanding of the spread of airborne pathogens. Furthermore, the differences identified in our study are expected to be relevant to a broader range of enclosed settings beyond urban buses.

The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect involves a rise in Spin-Orbit Coupling near a strong spin-orbit material's interface with an adjacent layer. This phenomenon has been observed in various systems, such as graphene and ferromagnetic layers, and controlling Spin-Orbit Coupling may lead to the discovery of novel phases in superconductor and semimetallic systems. In the present study, we investigate the Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect in Cobalt and Bismuth multilayers, and find that Spin-Orbit Coupling becomes weaker in Cobalt as the Bismuth layer thickness increases. A fit to the data yields an effective spin-orbit lambda of 0.1eV in a Cobalt layer of infinite thickness. By applying the Landau level formula, we obtain an effective lambda of 0.0999995eV, which matches the expected value. The research indicates that interface scattering plays a crucial role in determining the Spin-Orbit Coupling, and interface engineering may provide a way to improve this effect. Notably, we observe multiple Landau levels in the Bismuth bands due to the reduced number of available states in the confined system.

This paper provides approximate solutions to the fractional time-independent Schrödinger equation in $N$-dimensional space for a generalised Mie-type potential, expressed as $V(r^{\alpha})=A/r^{2\alpha} + B/r^{\alpha} + C$, with the fractional parameter $\alpha$ affecting the space variable $r$. As $\alpha$ equals 1, the potential becomes the original Mie-type potential, commonly studied in physics. Using the Jumarie type fractional derivative approach, solutions are obtained and expressed in terms of the fractional confluent Hypergeometric function. Verification of results is achieved by comparison with existing methods, particularly the fractional Adomian decomposition method (FADM). Additionally, numerical examples are presented and visualised through graphical representations for various values of $\alpha$ in both attractive and repulsive cases. Notably, exact solutions for the fractional time-independent Schrödinger equation are derived for this potential in $N$-dimensional space.

We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity, as it pertains to input sensitivity, affects its performance. In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant, taking into consideration various $p$-norms commonly used. This approach enables us to frame training a neural network with a limited Lipschitz constant as an optimisation problem that can be resolved via constrained stochastic gradient descent. Through our experiments, we found that models trained using this approach consistently performed better than those using alternative methods of regularisation. We further found that selecting hyperparameters is relatively straightforward and demonstrated the relationship between chosen norms and the resulting model's performance. The benefits of our approach are especially apparent when neural networks are trained on limited datasets.

We investigate the possibility of lepton-flavour non-universality in certain processes at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). To this end, we focus on Drell-Yan ditau production and calculate precise corrections to this process, taking into account the effects of quantum chromodynamics at the next-to-leading order. A specialized code is developed to efficiently handle these corrections, allowing for more accurate simulations of LHC collisions. By applying this code, we can compare our theoretical predictions with experimental data from the LHC and search for clues of new physics, such as vector leptoquarks, in the pattern of ditau production cross-sections.

Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower doses or shortened scan times. Deep-learning models have made significant advancements in enhancing PET images by translating low-quality PET scans with associated MRI data to higher-quality PET images, particularly with significantly reduced doses. Nonetheless, such deep learning approaches have primarily focused on utilizing training datasets similar to their test data, neglecting performance evaluation for new acquisitions outside of their distribution. We developed a novel neural network framework that incorporates the physics underlying the PET imaging process and estimates output uncertainty to address these limitations. This new uncertainty-aware neural network framework can utilize low-dose PET scans and accompanying MRI data to generate high-quality PET images at standard doses, thus enhancing robustness when processing out-of-distribution data, such as various forms of OOD PET-MRI acquisitions. Experimental results confirm the advantages of this model in enhancing PET images both quantitatively and qualitatively in various settings.

A linguistic analysis known as centering theory (CT) explains how coherence in conversations emerges from the connections between successive statements. This paper explores the link between CT and advanced computer systems that identify relationships within a text. By developing specific metrics and a search-based method, the study examines if modern computer models of textual connections are aligned with the principles of CT, particularly the concept of "directionality" and "shift" within the relationships. The analysis reveals that while some models of textual connections consider the principles of CT, many fail to demonstrate this capability. Furthermore, the study finds that models which generate connections between the relationships and those that resolve them are more likely to produce connections that are consistent with CT. Additionally, the study discusses the limitations and possible avenues for further investigation of the models' ability to resolve the connections.

Recently, WiFi has become the primary method for locating individuals or devices within indoor settings. To facilitate this process, WiFi fingerprinting, a technique where reference measurements with known locations are collected and analyzed, has become a standard approach in positioning methods and algorithms discussed in academic literature. However, measuring spatial distances between these collected data sets, also known as WiFi fingerprints, relies heavily on the choice of signal distance metric employed to map signal intensity to geographical distance. To address this issue, the researchers proposed using machine learning to enhance the estimation of geospatial distances between these data sets. This research analyzed 13 diverse datasets from various open sources in order to create a universally applicable model suitable for a wide range of indoor environments. The study discovered that a Random Forest model outperformed traditional distance metrics in the initial testing phase and, as shown in the second experiment, the proposed model could effectively generalize to new, unseen data sets without requiring retraining. Additionally, the model exhibited lower statistical distances from the mean compared to conventional methods, as demonstrated in the second experiment.

The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators and typically constrains the maximum beam current that can be achieved, especially for energy recovery linacs with multiple passes where a small amount of charge can generate a large beam current. Studies have highlighted the impact of filling patterns and recirculation schemes on beam and RF system interactions in multi-pass energy recovery linacs. This paper delves deeper into this subject by examining how filling patterns influence beam breakup instability and explores opportunities to optimize design for reduced instability effects. A theoretical beam-RF interaction model along with numerical modeling demonstrates that threshold currents can differ by 2-4 factors or even more, depending on machine design parameters. Consequently, carefully selecting filling patterns can delay the onset of beam breakup, enhancing the potential applications of future energy recovery linacs.

To extend the BFKL equation to NNLL accuracy, we need the complete set of NNLO vertex functions describing two gluons. Our research focuses on calculating the $\mathcal{O}(s)$-contributions to this function. We utilized the effective field theory approach with a one-loop calculation, utilizing packages such as青色, mass, and form. Our results can be integrated into existing implementations of the BFKL dynamics. Notably, we found an $s \to \infty$ contribution from the two-gluon contact interaction, which was previously unidentified in the literature, which is crucial for correctly representing the BFKL dynamics at large distances.

Theories explaining highly elongated polymer brush properties have provided valuable insights into the behavior of surface-grafted polymers in various scenarios. However, the parabolic model falls short in accurately describing elongated brushes on the surfaces of curved, concave substrates, like nanoparticles or certain types of block copolymer interfaces. Previous research has demonstrated that curved, stretched brushes necessitate a zone devoid of free chain ends and demands a revised theoretical analysis. Although the 'end exclusion zone' concept has been successfully incorporated into models for cylindrical and spherical surfaces, its implications for curved surfaces with varied geometries have yet to be explored. In this study, we introduce a revised strong-stretching theory that applies to molten polymer brushes on curved surfaces of any complexity. By utilizing an variational approach and comparing the free energies of brushes on planar and curved surfaces, we determine the end exclusion zone size. Our findings reveal that this zone emerges only when the curvature radius falls below a critical threshold related to the polymer chain's persistence length. Additionally, we observe that the zone size increases as surface curvature rises and decreases with higher monomer densities or molecular weights. The results derived from this revised model were validated through direct molecular dynamics simulations, demonstrating its efficacy in accurately describing the behavior of brushes on curved surfaces of various geometries, including plane, cylinder, and sphere surfaces.

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph.

Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning image processing algorithms, applying them to all-sky maps generated by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. To simulate a year's worth of observations, they employed dictionary learning, U-net, and Noise2Noise algorithms on just one week of data. The machine learning-based method enhanced the image quality compared to standard techniques, particularly in replicating complex diffuse emissions from the galactic plane. These models can simplify image analysis by sidestepping assumptions about emission patterns, yet they also struggle with temporally varying sources, like blazars, which change significantly over a year. Despite this limitation, this approach shows promise for automatically identifying these sources and detecting transient phenomena and giant structures often missed in focused observations.

Inspired by the effectiveness of the serial dictatorship mechanism in resolving group decision-making challenges, we investigate its potential for solving a range of combinatorial optimization problems by employing a basic model where multiple agents take sequential actions. The model stipulates that each agent chooses their optimal action based on the actions taken by previous agents in the predetermined order. We aim to identify action sequences that maximize overall benefit for all agents involved. We establish theoretical bounds on achievable social welfare when employing a query-based approach and find that this results in a marginally improved approximation of optimal social welfare when considering a general scenario. However, when applied to a range of combinatorial optimization methods, including matchings, Knapsack problems, and Maximum Weight Independent Sets, we demonstrate the superiority of the serial dictatorship approach in achieving a significant level of approximation. We further examine the limited efficacy of this approach when employing a randomized strategy. In contrast, we reveal the primacy of the serial dictatorship approach by showing that it can achieve a substantial level of approximation, specifically a $2-O(1)$ factor, when compared to any combinatorial optimization method that access input a general sequence.

We designed two distinct point spread function (PSF) analysis techniques 
for detecting wide binary asteroids within wide field surveys, and subsequently
applied these to Pan-STARRS1 images featuring main belt asteroids spanning 
four color bands, which yield independent estimates of object sizes. For 
each individual field of view, we computed the gravitational parameter from
the orbital periods and distances of binary asteroids, and gr size ratios from 
the slope of the object's spectral energy distribution. By correlating these 
parameters, we were able to identify candidate binary asteroids across different 
fields of view, and verified four of these candidates through astrometric 
observations and orbital reconstruction. Among confirmed binaries, one was 
present in only a single field of view, and the other three appeared in 
two or more fields. These discoveries have larger semi-major axes compared 
to known binary asteroids, and compared to single asteroids that showed 
periodic variations in their brightness.

This research supplements the findings related to the specified context, model, and estimation methods initially presented by Auerbach in 2019. The paper's first section explores the asymptotic behavior of the estimators presented in section 2 of the Auerbach's work. The second section investigates extensions to the model. The third section applies the model to estimate peer effects within networks. The fourth section presents results obtained from simulated data.

This study introduces novel versions of the Leibniz Rule for the Riemann-Liouville Variable-Order fractional integral and derivative. It derives key formulas, including product, quotient, and chain rules for both the integral and differential operators. Specifically, four distinct product rule formulas, four quotient rule formulas derived from product rule types, and four chain rule formulas have been established.

We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, which can be evaluated through the lens of a role-playing game.
Our methodology combines a specialized D&D theory-of-mind framework with a reinforcement learning-based conversation guide approach, and we extend this hybrid model进one person's mental capabilities using a sophisticated artificial intelligence.

The intricate relationship between protein knots and their folding processes is an area that biologists are actively trying to comprehend. Recent research categorizes the spatial arrangements of knotted proteins using advanced topological models. A novel statistical approach, inspired by topological principles, enables the comparison of knotted protein structures based on their spatial projections. This analysis uncovers the distinctions in geometry among proteins with trefoil knots and also identifies clustering patterns according to their sequence similarities. By focusing on the intrinsic properties of these proteins in their natural state, this research uncovers various folding pathways for trefoil knots and reveals that proteins with shallow knots follow a distinct pathway compared to those with deep knots. Specifically, this method uncovers the pattern where proteins with shallow knots exhibit an initial chain compaction in an non-native state, in contrast to those with deep knots displaying pre-formed local structures. This finding is considered an innovative hypothesis that may apply to the folding processes of other complex proteins.

Let $\omega$ be a Kaehler form on the real $4$-dimensional torus $T^4$. Given that it fulfills an irrationality criterion which can be realized via an arbitrarily minor adjustment of $\omega$, this note proves that the smoothly trivial symplectic mapping class group of the one-point symplectic blowup of $(T^4,\omega)$ is countably infinite.

A detailed investigation of the anomalous Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem has been undertaken with an emphasis on its underlying mathematical structures drawn from Lie algebras, geometry, and number theory. The principles behind the anomalous NG theorem have been explored using both local Lie algebras and global Lie groups. In analyzing this phenomenon, a quasi-Heisenberg algebra was discovered in a variety of symmetry breaking scenarios associated with the anomalous NG theorem. Notably, this algebraic structure can cause deviations from the conventional Heisenberg uncertainty principle, which could potentially be experimentally verified. A framework for effective potential formalism was developed to better understand the mechanisms driving the anomalous NG theorem. A study of a bosonic kaon condensation model incorporating a finite chemical potential served as an explicit example of Lorentz-symmetry breaking. A general discussion on the anomalous NG theorem has been presented through the lens of this model's Lagrangian approach. Moreover, this investigation uncovered both the conditions necessary and sufficient for true NG boson generation as well as the mechanism for breaking the symmetry of the vacuum. Effectively, this means that in any Lagrangian theory, true NG bosons are generated if and only if the vacuum expectation value of a current carries a non-zero value. Finally, insights into possible applications of the anomalous NG theorem in both particle and condensed matter physics have been presented.

Recent studies indicate that augmenting data with counterfactual knowledge can enable models to grasp a task's causal framework, thereby producing resilient and versatile models. Nonetheless, the scale and variety of such counterfactual data are restricted when sourced from crowds and become costly to extend to new perturbation types when produced through supervised methods. To address this limitation, we propose a novel, unsupervised Counterfactual Data Selection Framework based on a Large Language Model that identifies high-value explanatory phrases from a massive corpus. By distilling these phrases and applying them to a target dataset, we observe a range of improvements in subsequent training stages, as demonstrated in our experimental analysis. Specifically, our findings show that our selected phrases, when incorporated into the a) Causal Explanation's text and b) Task's alternative description, result in a 10.35% and 7.65% average gain in prediction accuracy, respectively, as per the robustness and generalizability of our findings.

Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. Many instances are instead attributed to contaminants between graphene and the substrate, or alternative processes such as van der Waals epitaxy. This study discovered that when growing the Heusler compound GdPtSb on clean graphene substrates, it results in a unique 30 degree rotated superstructure, not explicable through other mechanisms. This rotation domain percentage significantly increases at lower growth temperatures. It's suggested that slower surface diffusion at lower temperatures favors the remote epitaxial process over faster surface diffusion at higher temperatures. Moreover, this study demonstrated that precise annealing of the graphene and consideration of film/substrate lattice mismatches are necessary for achieving epitaxial relationships with a range of Heusler compounds, including LaPtSb and GdAuGe. The distinctive 30 degree rotated superstructure offers a potential experimental signature for identifying remote epitaxy.

A code is referred to as $ \Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear if it results from a particular type of encoding process called the Gray image of a code that has properties derived from $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-additive code, given a prime number p greater than two. This paper specifically delves into the examination of the rank and dimension of the kernel of $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes. Furthermore, specific limits for the rank of $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes have been established and the conditions under which these limits can be achieved are described. In addition, the minimum possible value for the dimension of the kernel of $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes has been identified and the conditions under which this value can be reached are also described. As a part of this research, the additive code with the maximum rank of the associated $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear code and the code with the minimum dimension of the kernel of the associated $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear code have been constructed.

Conditional GANs have demonstrated superior performance in tasks requiring the generation of specific classes.  However, creating training data with multiple labels to control multiple conditions simultaneously proves impractical due to the extensive annotation required, a problem that limits the availability of such datasets in real-world applications.  This paper investigates a new setting called the single positive scenario, in which each piece of data is marked by only a single relevant label without any additional information regarding potential irrelevant labels.  A novel technique known as single-to-multi-label sampling was developed to generate multi-label data based on this single positive label annotation.  This new approach is a supplemental tool that allows current unconditional and conditional GANs to generate high-quality multi-label data while significantly reducing the required annotation. Experimental findings with real image datasets demonstrate that the technique can effectively produce accurate multi-label data even in comparison to a model trained using comprehensive datasets.

The GNS construction forms a correspondence between abstract collections of physical observables in a C*-algebra and associated physical states. This process essentially amounts to a reverse operation to obtain the algebra given a state. We demonstrate that the GNS construction behaves as a kind of inverse procedure for state representation through an abstract adjoint relationship, capturing fundamental aspects of the algebra's underlying properties. This abstract adjoint relationship must be seen within the context of weakly natural transformations, a concept that arises from categorifying functors. This formulation of the relationship provides the basis for interpreting the inherent mathematical structure in physical terms.

The cause of gamma-rays in nearby galaxies that produce in significant amounts is still unclear.  In these galaxies, gamma-rays originate from the high-energy processes taking place near the supermassive black hole. There are two main theories: one posits that gamma-rays result from jets emerging from the black hole, and the other suggests that gamma-rays are produced by a magnetic field structure known as a magnetically arrested disk (MAD). This paper presents a new method for identifying MADs by detecting a specific relationship between radio and X-ray emissions. This method is particularly useful for gamma-ray data as well. We also propose that the low-energy cutoff of gamma-rays can be traced back to the properties of the associated magnetic field. This can be observed as a correlation between radio emissions at different energy levels (specifically, $\nu F_{\nu}$ at 100 times lower and 10 times higher frequencies). This pattern is seen in about half of the gamma-ray galaxies and provides evidence for the presence of magnetic fields around the black hole, providing the first direct evidence of MADs emitting gamma-rays. This evidence applies to a variety of high-energy gamma-ray sources, and provides a framework for understanding the gamma-rays in galaxies like M51, NGC 4302, and NGC 610.

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and the variability of recording devices.  To address this challenge, this study investigates the development of effective methods to analyze cardiac auscultation sounds that have been affected by both types of distortions.  After conducting mathematical analyses of noise effects on feature extraction techniques, the authors propose using a combination of linear and logarithmic spectral features to aid a deep learning-based classifier.  The proposed method, which utilizes a Residual Neural Network (ResNet) and was tested on noisy recordings obtained from multiple stethoscopes, demonstrates a significant improvement in accuracy compared to existing approaches.  The proposed technique achieves the best results across a wide range of recording conditions and environments, indicating its potential for low-cost implementation.  The findings provide a framework for creating cardiac auscultation systems capable of accurately diagnosing conditions even in noisy environments using low-cost devices.

The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. Successful smart healthcare relies on training machine learning models using a large quantity of user data, but several key challenges arise. Primarily, user data exists in disparate segments, complicating data aggregation without breaching privacy protocols. Secondly, models trained on cloud platforms struggle to accommodate personalization requirements. This paper introduces FedHealth, a pioneering federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare designed to address these difficulties. FedHealth aggregates data via federated learning and employs transfer learning to develop personalized models. It succeeds in providing accurate, personalized healthcare without compromising security and data confidentiality. Experimentation reveals that FedHealth yields 5.3% greater accuracy in wearable activity recognition when compared to conventional approaches. Furthermore, FedHealth demonstrates versatility, extensibility, and vast potential applications in the healthcare industry.

This study classifies portfolio optimization strategies with higher order moments including skewness and kurtosis to aid Hedge Fund practitioners in navigating various paradigms and methodologies. Key research approaches, such as utility theory and multi-objective optimization, are reviewed, with an examination of their benefits and limitations.

In large-scale organizations, recruiting involves interviewing a substantial number of applicants, a time-consuming and intricate process. To achieve efficiency, a well-planned approach to selection is crucial. This process comprises two main aspects: interviewing and choosing the right candidates for further rounds of interviews. This paper concentrates on addressing the problem of automatically choosing candidates for interviews. We model this process as an optimization problem, where the goal is to choose candidates whose profiles match a specific job requirement while a limited set of constraints, including a fixed budget and allocated time, are met. This decision-making process can be formulated as a constrained mixed integer knapsack problem, a variant of which has been proven to be NP-complete. To solve this challenge, we propose a two-step approach. In the first step, we use a gradient method to find a solution that closely meets our requirements. In the second step, we employ an efficient algorithm to recover the most suitable integer solution. To validate our method, we conducted numerical experiments comparing it to existing approaches. We also developed a web-based platform to illustrate our method's practical application in a real-world scenario.

This study tackles a complex control issue, where the costs of transitioning between states can change suddenly in time. Our main achievement is to derive multiple ways to characterize the optimal cost function, as well as to demonstrate the existence of policies that minimize costs under this dynamic framework. Alongside, we examine the existence and distinctiveness of solutions to a system of stochastic differential equations featuring abrupt obstacles, whose characteristics depend on the unknown solution and vary discontinuously on the real line. This system's analysis is supported by the use of a stochastic tensorial driver, whose existence and uniqueness are also established in this paper.

To explore the significance of new physics, our research investigates asymmetric leptoquark pair creation in the Large Hadron Collider to provide solid constraints on its properties and suggest possible ways to produce leptoquarks in a pure state for experiments. Asymmetric production arises from the interaction of a leptoquark with a quark from the opposing beam. This process can result in the production of a pair of leptoquarks with different flavors or the same type but differing in their mass. We analyze the properties of this process, focusing on the leptoquark mass that ranges from 1TeV to 4TeV, and the possible values of the coupling between the leptoquark and the Higgs boson, which are within the limits set by current experiments. To do this, we simulate the physical outcomes of these reactions using a combination of Pythia 8 and FeynArf/Heraf++ within the scope of the Large Hadron Collider.

We analyzed a sample of 106 galaxies for which data is available for two specific fine structure lines of neutral atomic carbon, and we found their average conditions to be significantly non-equilibrium. Based on exact solutions of a 3-level system without any assumptions regarding hydrogen gas properties, we found the line formation mechanism to be influenced by non-LTE (local thermodynamic equilibrium) excitation. This non-equilibrium state may explain recent observations of gas temperatures around 25K and is not correlated with actual gas temperatures. It also hampers our ability to estimate molecular gas temperatures based on carbon isotope lines and contributes uncertainty in mass estimates for molecular gas. However, this line ratio is valuable in modeling both CO and CI spectra and is independent of radiative transfer models. It is also proposed that extreme starbursts with low line ratios and high dust temperatures could be associated with massive low-density winds and/or gas reservoirs. If verified by further imaging, this may provide an indicator for identifying such reservoirs.

Levenshtein initially introduced the sequence reconstruction problem in 2001.
It deals with a scenario in which the same sequence from a specific set undergoes
different channel transmissions and yields distinct outputs at a decoder.
Assuming that the original transmitted sequence maintains a distance of d from a particular code
and includes at most r errors per channel, the sequence reconstruction task is
determining the least amount of transmission channels needed to obtain an accurate
replica of the original transmitted sequence.
It's also essential to note that this number must surpass the maximum possible
overlap between two spheres in a metric with a radius r, where these two spheres
have centers that are at least d units apart.
In this research paper, we examine the sequence reconstruction problem for permutations
under a specific distance metric known as the Hamming distance.
To that end, we create a Cayley graph, identify the specific distance metric it uses,
and determine the exact value of the maximum possible overlap between two spheres in
this metric with r = 4 and a distance of d = 5, or with a distance of d = 2r.

Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments will be capable of detecting gravitational waves produced by individual supermassive black hole binaries moving in highly elliptical orbits. By comparing various methods for computing PTA signals from these binaries, our findings indicate that employing approximate analytic expressions yields the most efficient computation, leading to a significant reduction of up to 50 times in computational costs compared to other methods. The accuracy of these analytic expressions is validated through a relevant mismatch metric and found to be sufficiently precise for the PTA parameter space of interest. Furthermore, we introduce an improved approach using spline interpolation to enhance the computation speed for specific narrow-band PTA datasets. The implementation of these findings in the GWecc package enables seamless access to searching for such eccentric signals within PTA datasets via the ENTERPRISE platform.

We establish that in ASEP, a system with initial data represented by discrete steps, a second-class particle placed at the origin, will asymptotically converge to a velocity whose probability distribution is uniform across the interval $[-1,1]$ as time tends to infinity. This conclusive finding addresses two unresolved conjectures from "The TASEP speed process" and enables us to develop the ASEP speed process.

This study examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic to address pressing issues affecting public health policy and understanding of epidemic dynamics. Beginning with an overview of fundamental Kermack-McKendrick model characteristics, we delve into generalized models, considering applications such as network structures, simultaneous transmission of viruses, the patterns of epidemic curve growth, probability distributions, and critical time periods for model compartment analysis. A unified framework emerges, emphasizing the critical role that context, drawing from epidemiology, medicine, and biology, plays in informing both model development and analysis. Failing to consider the biological implications of mathematical models during data fitting risks producing statistically significant results, but lacking practical significance for guiding pandemic management, mitigation, and eventual control.

We have theoretically analyzed multiple facets of coherent atom-molecule conversion in systems with one spin unit and Bose-Einstein condensates. Focusing on suitable dark-state conditions, we found that the interplay between collisions that transfer spin and light-based association results in stable atom-molecule pair formation from initial spinless atoms through two-body interactions equivalent to an effective three-body recombination. In our study, we also investigate the impact of light-based association and initial magnetization when a precise condition is met. Furthermore, we explored two scenarios: one in which the dark state condition is met imperfectly, either generally known as the adiabatic case, or not at all. In the adiabatic case, we derived an inelastic non-rigid pendulum model, which enables discussion on magnetic instability in an "atom-molecule pendulum" as well as the phenomenon of "atom-molecule phase transition" when the initial magnetization exceeds a critical level. When the dark state condition is not met, we discovered that three-body recombination can be understood as two successive two-body recombination steps, potentially forming diatomic molecules with unusual properties.

Our proposed DNA-storage system presents a new, flexible structure that establishes a hierarchical relationship among data objects identified by the same primer pair and facilitates efficient data revisions. Unlike existing approaches, in this architecture a pair of twenty base PCR primers no longer defines a singular object, but rather a distinct, independently managed storage segment with its own index. We've discovered that, although there are limited sets of primer pairs compatible with one another, each segment offers essentially limitless internal storage capacity. Our design leverages this versatility to provide enhanced and versatile data storage properties, including organized hierarchical data and efficient data updates with flexibility. Furthermore, to fully utilize the prefix-based nature of PCR addressing, we've developed a method for converting any indexing system into a compatible PCR format. This enables us to utilize primers that can be variably extended to include desired parts of the index, allowing us to precisely locate specific objects within a segment with minimal scope, resulting in the reduction of sequencing costs by up to 140x for the retrieval of smaller data objects.

Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, their traditional numerical solutions can be time-consuming and require precise riverbed measurements. In this research, a two-step process is proposed to tackle this issue. Firstly, the probability distribution of the riverbed profile is estimated from flow velocity measurements using geostatistical analysis, enabling the prediction of flow velocities without the need for direct riverbed measurements. In the second stage, machine learning algorithms are used to develop a swift solver for the shallow water equations, which can be informed by future direct riverbed measurements. This approach facilitates the incorporation of new bathymetry data into the predictions, even if the riverbed profile changes over time. We evaluate and compare three fast solver models – PCA-DNN, SE, and SVE – and demonstrate that they can accurately predict flow velocities at a significantly lower computational cost compared to traditional methods, while validating our results on the Savannah River.

HDR photography combines multiple photos captured at various exposure levels
to produce an image with an expanded dynamic range. Our proposed method
automates this image synthesis process for such images by leveraging deep
learning techniques and presents two main advantages: it streamlines image
capture by using a single photo for exposure reference and it offers
guardrails to prevent unnatural image content. Our method automatically
determines the best exposure setting by considering the image's content and
modifies areas that are too dark or overexposed in non-standard HDR images.
To train the model, we manually gathered image pairs consisting of bracketed
photos and their corresponding content-controlled HDR versions, resulting in a
new dataset called Mobile-HDR. Experimentally, our method demonstrates
superior image quality compared to current techniques, delivers a
user-friendly experience on mobile devices, it is efficient enough to
synthesize images in real-time on a CPU and it is robust against images
captured at different exposure settings.

Causal deep learning, an emerging and significant area within the broader field of machine learning, aims to integrate causal knowledge into deep learning models through a flexible representation framework. This will lead to more accurate and generalizable predictions and inferences, though significant hurdles remain due to the diverse nature of methods within the field. A new publication addresses this challenge by categorizing methods within causal deep learning, refining Pearl's causal hierarchy while considering parametric assumptions and input/representation structures. The resulting framework provides researchers with a map for benchmarking, comparing methods, and identifying knowledge gaps across machine learning disciplines, such as supervised learning, reinforcement learning, and generative modeling. The authors open-source this framework for the research community to use, with potential applications in guiding related work sections and highlighting paper contributions.

This note presents a new category of map functions known as oriented colored broken submersions, which forms the most basic type of map functions that adhere to the b-principle, and is nearly equivalent to the set of oriented submersions in 2 dimensions. It demonstrates that the Madsen-Weiss theorem, which can be viewed as a variation of the standard Mumford Conjecture, is derivable from a specific application of the b-principle to oriented colored broken submersions, combined with the findings from Harer's stability theorem and Miller and Morita's work.

This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity, researchers have been able to effectively utilize BDDC and AMG multilevel preconditioners to solve these problems. A key challenge addressed in this research is solving the large systems of nonlinear equations that arise from this process, which can be accomplished using a combination of the Newton method, reduced integration, and a variety of solver techniques. To ensure the scalability of these solutions, research was conducted using a range of computational grids and up to 128 processors, utilizing the BDDC method in conjunction with BoomerAMG and a strong-strong multigrid method. To better understand the mechanical behavior of the heart, researchers have been able to utilize a 2D time-evolving model of rat ventricular mechanics as well as 3D models of rat and mouse ventricular mechanics, which can be found in previous studies.

Standard diffusion models can fail, particularly when influenced by correlations and variations, where mean squared displacements grow in a linear manner with time. We investigate the spread of a fractional Brownian population exhibiting time-dependent and diverse diffusion characteristics. Our primary objective is to establish the relationship between these individual characteristics and the population's spatial distribution as observed over time. We examine the applicability and limitations of this approach to a broad category of self-similar diffusion processes, utilizing a general framework that is subsequently applied to recognized processes such as Laplace diffusion, nonlinear diffusion, and their variants.

A fundamental theory is developed to describe both linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions between the modes of dielectric optical resonators, with the assumption that the material's refractive index changes in a specific way. The mode coupling coefficients arising from the Kerr effect are shown to result directly from the third-order susceptibility. The theory is applied to a range of devices and materials, including all-optical switches and logic gates based on the cross-phase modulation effect. Embyrric dimensions are in a range of tens to hundreds of micrometers.

A recent study proposes a novel deep learning approach that utilizes generative adversarial networks to generate highly detailed turbulent velocity patterns from limited-resolution data across a range of Reynolds numbers. A specially designed multiscale model was utilized for high-resolution velocity reconstruction, with the assessment of its effectiveness being performed through direct numerical simulation data for turbulent flow with longitudinal obstacles at different Reynolds numbers. The evaluation showed that this deep learning framework accurately replicates high-resolution velocity patterns and statistical measures from two low-resolution data sets. Furthermore, it was observed that this model successfully recreates turbulent velocity patterns at Reynolds numbers that it was not originally trained on.

Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic, ever-changing problems common in critical domains such as robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle with new tasks outside their training data. To address this challenge, the focus is shifting towards innovative, real-world applicable algorithms that can conquer the problems posed by unfamiliar environments. In order to develop and evaluate cutting-edge methods in this field, simulation tools are needed to compile diverse, real-world data for modeling. In response, we introduce Reinforcement Learning Explorator (RLE), a comprehensive and versatile assessment platform designed to evaluate algorithms for lifelong learning. It features a robust and modular architecture, integrating a comprehensive set of evaluations and an integrated data management system. The latest iteration, RLE2, enhances functionality and usability, providing an open and user-friendly environment for researchers. It is also accompanied by a study examining the challenges of lifelong learning in varying environments and the development of a cutting-edge algorithm, which has been applied in the lifelong learning tests compiled in RLE2. The source code for RLE2 is made available to the public.

Understanding business processes relies on process discovery methods, analyzing data trails to reveal underlying processes. As processes evolve over time, their corresponding models must adapt, otherwise they may inaccurately predict future behaviors. Our approach develops an algorithm to identify processes from event flows, represented as Dynamic Condition Response (DCR) graphs, providing temporal process data and subsequently declarative process models. We validate this method through experiments and analyses, comparing it to transforming processes to non-temporal graphs before applying standard discovery techniques. Our approach also highlights the importance of ensuring process data aligns with the expected accuracy of the resulting declarative model. We illustrate this approach through an in-depth financial example and associated dataset.
This note provides an introduction to the interplay between Hodge-theoretic and geometric approaches to compactifying moduli spaces of algebraic varieties.

Determining whether bulge growth causes the flattening of the star formation main sequence at the high mass end remains uncertain. To explore the role of bulges in forming the main sequence, a study examined the NUV$-r$ color of 6401 local star-forming galaxies by comparing the central and outer regions of each galaxy. Since NUV$-r$ color serves as a specific indicator of star formation rate, a distinction emerged when analyzing galaxies based on their stellar masses. At stellar masses less than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, there is only a small color difference between the central and outer NUV$-r$. Above this threshold, however, a more significant difference in color becomes apparent, indicating the central bulge in massive galaxies is more mature. Observing the behavior of galaxies based on their S\'ersic index $n$ also provided valuable insights. Those with an index of 2.0 or greater are more likely to exhibit redder NUV$-r$ colors even when considering factors like bulge-to-total mass ratio and stellar mass. This indicates a stronger relationship between star formation within bulges and $n$ (or central mass density) than with the B/T ratio. This paper conducts a sentiment analysis across languages, examining the
emotional content of news articles using both few-shot and zero-shot learning
techniques. The primary objective is to categorize Croatian news articles as
expressing positive, negative, or neutral sentiment, employing a dataset from
Slovene. The underlying model is a multilingual BERT-based system, pre-trained
on three languages: English, Slovene, and Croatian. The paper investigates
various setups utilizing datasets from two languages and presents a straightforward
multi-task model to accomplish sentiment classification. The assessment involves
zero-shot and few-shot learning approaches within single-task and multi-task
experiments for both Slovene and Croatian.

X-ray images contain subtle characteristics with predictive information about patients who are likely to experience severe symptoms, require oxygen therapy, may develop respiratory failure, and are at risk of requiring intensive care. A study involving 1,660 COVID-19 patients' chest X-rays used a deep learning model to identify these subtle features that could forecast ICU admission. Researchers extracted 500 important features from the learned image representations and used them to predict which patients were going to require intensive care, with results showing high accuracy in these predictions. Furthermore, the predicted probabilities of ICU admission were correlated with actual patient data, revealing image features correlated with severe symptoms, oxygen therapy requirements, respiratory failure, and other critical health indicators. These findings suggest that such predicted features may help medical professionals make more informed decisions and support the development of early warning systems for identifying high-risk patients.

The classical universal bundle functor W mapping from the category of simplicial groups in C to the category of simplicial sets in C lifts to a monadic structure on the category of simplicial groups in C, and this extension holds for simplicial algebras defined by any Lawvere theory that includes group theory.

This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. By employing this strategy, BNPS yields an optimized model performance and a notable decrease in false positives. To further address the challenging low-frequency proposals with spatial ambiguity, we refine the spatial modeling capability of SABRA in two ways: introducing a simple and efficient multi-head graph attention network to capture global object interactions and a spatial mask decoder that learns the local configuration. Our approach demonstrates superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art methods across three datasets for human-object interaction and visual relationship detection.

We've performed an in-depth analysis of three galaxy cores at $\rm z=2.91$ within a massive galaxy group, yielding high-resolution infrared and submillimeter data. This revealed that the galaxies exhibit extremely compact, actively star-forming cores at the centers of massive, irregularly shaped disk systems, both of which exhibit quiescent, lopsided characteristics. Consequently, these galaxies are witnessing `outside-in' quenching. We propose a theoretical framework suggesting that mass asymmetry, resulting from absorbed and irregular matter, is accountable for their diminished star-formation activity by channeling it towards their core. Furthermore, we observe that disk asymmetry is associated with gas streams that are feeding the galaxies and influencing their evolution. This is manifested by an alignment of the galaxies' major axes with the nearby inflowing tidal tails. This study is indicative of galaxies developing bulges through `major' mergers, which are redirecting angular momentum and decoupling massive, galaxy-core systems from the rest of the rotating disk system, leading to continued, internal star-formation activity, but at a diminished rate. We contend, therefore, that many galaxy-core systems are isolated, isolated entities, observing, therefore, star-formation activity, but, at a, diminished, rate.,

Recently discovered solar observations from Bolivia (5250 m above sea level) and Mexico (4600 m above sea level) uncovered a significant event on November 7, 2004, linked to a powerful X2.0 solar flare. Analysis of recorded data, along with satellite observations from GOES 11 and SOHO, suggest that neutrons may have broken down into electrons and protons. Historically, evidence of this process was found on board ISEE3 on June 3rd, 1982 and through ground detectors in Goose Bay and Deep River on October 19th, 1989, providing a second terrestrial instance of this occurrence.

This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex angular momentum redistribution
mechanism within a Be star, specifically $\gamma$ Cassiopeiae, during a recent
"Be-state" phase. Contrary to typical Be star behavior, the star's rotation period
has accelerated from 85.4 days to 80.6 days over a 12-day observation interval,
with the magnitude of this change far exceeding any known angular momentum
transport expectation for Be stars. We propose two possible explanations for this
anomalous behavior: either the star is in close proximity to a giant planet at a
100-day orbit, likely contributing to this specific rotation rate change; or, it
indicates the existence of yet-unknown mechanisms capable of redistributing
angular momentum on a stellar surface. Consequently, $\gamma$ Cas may be a pivotal
target for observations using next-generation high-accuracy instruments, such as
the Extremely Large Telescopes, in search of modes breaking stellar adiabatic
timescales.

Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm worldwide. Although machine learning models have been employed to identify false information, the vulnerability to data poisoning attacks remains a significant challenge.
To tackle this limitation, an emergent fake news classifier is proposed that leverages common sense knowledge found in social media content. Furthermore, a novel meta-learning framework is developed to create fake news classifiers with excellent generalization abilities on unknown data.
The proposed method, called Meta-NPN, uses a small amount of text-image pair data from web crawlers as a shared knowledge base. By treating label generation as a neural process, the Meta-NPN framework facilitates the learning of fake news detectors through the meta-optimization of a generator network.
The effectiveness of the proposed Meta-NPN model is validated through a variety of tasks, including few-shot and normal supervised learning, as shown in experimental results.

This research paper examines a one-dimensional periodic transport equation, which involves non-local and non-convex interactions. We have identified specific conditions under which solutions to this equation develop singularities, as well as methods to predict and calculate the time period when these developments occur. Additionally, by analyzing and modifying potential functions, we have established a lower bound on the time when singularities develop, which is not dependent on the strength of interactions and is, in turn, used to create a precise prediction for the development of singularities in this equation.

Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained popularity due to their utility in omnidirectional precoding techniques. This research extends Golay complementary matrices to higher dimensions, presenting novel construction methods for complex-valued binary and unitary Golay complementary matrices in both even and odd dimensions. Specific constructions include 2x2 and 2xn unitary Golay complementary matrices in even dimensions, an even dimension complex-valued binary GCM construction, side-length 3 unitary Golay complementary matrices, 3x3 and 3xunit complex-valued binary GCMs in even dimensions, as well as several other constructions in side-length 4 and 5 units. The properties of these higher dimensional units are examined and illustrated through graphical representations.

Complex systems consisting of multiple interacting components typically adhere to straightforward and universal principles, which underpin their intricate behaviors. Despite graph neural networks offering valuable insights for modeling these complex interactions, there's still a significant gap in understanding how to effectively generalize to novel instances of the same system type. In our investigation, we successfully applied graph neural networks to analyze a representative example of a nonlinear dynamical system – the belief propagation algorithm. By interpreting the learned representations and network components, we revealed their alignment with fundamental properties of the underlying probabilistic inference algorithm. Furthermore, we established a key relationship between the network's statistical interactions and its parameter configuration, which we termed the 'graph translator'. Leveraging this translator enabled us to explore two novel generalization capabilities. Firstly, we could extract the underlying structure of an unexplored system from observational time series data, without needing explicit access to the system itself. Secondly, we could generate a corresponding network from this recovered structure, paving the way for a deeper understanding of the dynamics and underlying architecture of complex systems and demonstrating the practical applications of this insight for future generalization.

We introduce an infinite family of recursive formulas for calculating the counts of binary integer partitions that fulfill specific divisibility criteria, establishing relationships among these counts via cumulative sums. These formulas have a meaningful interpretation within the framework of graded polynomial rings and enable us to derive computations related to homology modules in the context of stable homotopy theory, utilizing the properties of the mod $2$ Steenrod algebra.

A cutting-edge, minimally invasive therapy called Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) treats seizures caused by epilepsy in a specific brain area, the mesial temporal lobe. Evaluating the effectiveness of this treatment requires analyzing changes to the treated brain area after LITT, which can be achieved by accurately defining the treated region through image processing. Although deep learning techniques offer high precision in defining this region, training them requires a large amount of data which can be hard to obtain for a new and emerging treatment such as LITT. In response, this paper proposes an innovative framework called Progressive Brain Lesion Synthesis, consisting of multiple stages to artificially create more training data with various characteristics, thereby enhancing the precision of the therapy evaluation. Furthermore, the paper includes a design for encoding external information that can aid in training and improving segmentation results by integrating a condition and mask embedding block, resulting in better outcomes when compared to common image processing methods, according to experimental data.

GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, leveraging graph transformation rules to ease these tasks. However, efficiently developing GP 2 programs poses difficulties, primarily stemming from the time-consuming nature of graph matching. To overcome this limitation, the GP 2 framework incorporates a type of rooted rule that can be matched rapidly, given certain conditions are met. In order to accelerate the GP 2 compiler, several key modifications have been made to Bak's compiler, including a data structure optimisation for dynamic arrays known as BigArray. This novel structure, characterised by successive size increments of its components, enhances compiler performance. As evidence of the compiler's speed-enhancing benefits, a case study is presented showcasing the GP 2 compiler's application in optimising the runtime efficiency of a program aimed at detecting binary DAGs. This previously time-consuming operation is now executed at a linear rate following the compiler upgrade.

Dimensionality reduction in high-dimensional data is effectively managed by a technique called feature extraction. Self-supervised learning's prominent method, contrastive learning, has gained considerable interest recently. Our research introduces a novel, all-encompassing framework that integrates contrastive learning for both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction tasks. The framework's initial step constructs unique contrastive learning graphs to differentiate between similar and dissimilar data points, with a focus on optimizing a contrastive loss function to obtain the projection matrix. The framework's capability to handle similar and dissimilar data enables the integration of unsupervised and supervised feature extraction techniques. We further developed three specific methods: an unsupervised contrastive learning technique and two supervised contrastive learning approaches. Our framework's superiority is demonstrated through comprehensive numerical experiments conducted on five real-world datasets, resulting in performance improvements over existing methods.

We establish an infinite sequence of locally arc-transitive graphs characterized by a unique property: their automorphism groups partition vertices into two distinct orbits while exhibiting quasiprimativity on just one orbit, specifically within a class of twisted wreath structures. Our findings expand upon a framework initially proposed by Giudici, Li, and Praeger by providing an infinite number of examples classified under the star normal quotient twisted wreath category for locally arc-transitive graphs.

Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling becomes increasingly complex as the number of variables grows, as it typically requires a parameter for each category, making interpretation challenging. To address this issue, we developed an innovative penalized likelihood method based on a new form of group lasso penalty specifically tailored for categorical data, which determines the lasso penalty applied to each category's level based on its corresponding variable's group. We found through simulation studies that this new penalty produced sparse and interpretable models while maintaining high prediction accuracy comparable to models without variable selection. Furthermore, we successfully applied this method to identify a sparse model from a dataset of 116 chemical substances, pinning down the key levels of four critical variables associated with substance persistence in the environment.

Recent advances in large language models have achieved par or near-par performance with human experts in various natural language understanding tasks. When it comes to NLU benchmarks, these models display accurate grasp of basic common sense, sentences containing complex grammatical structures, and simple logical relations. However, when evaluating their performance on domain-specific knowledge, the results are mixed. This knowledge is usually acquired through a combine of backtranslation and masking techniques. Our proposed method, SKILL, incorporates structured data into the training of large language models to improve their understanding. We utilized three distinct structured formats including JSON, NatJSON, and XML as inputs for our learning process. When applied to eight different datasets, JSON and NatJSON formats yielded the most effective outcomes. Our findings reveal that using structured data can lead to significant improvements in the performance of large language models.

Achieving a seamless visual experience and optimal system performance when displaying line joins on vector maps requires an efficient anti-aliasing technique. However, the limitations of OpenGL API hinder optimal rendering results when approximating the anti-aliased effect through multiple triangles. In an attempt to rectify this issue, this study introduces a straightforward yet high-performance algorithm utilizing two triangles to replicate fan-shaped line joins via alpha operation. Our findings indicate this technique yields a genuine anti-aliasing effect while reducing memory consumption, raising frame rates, and preventing overlap rendering in map visualization. Our novel anti-aliasing method has been applied in notable applications such as Tencent Mobile Maps and Tencent Automotive Maps.

To improve modeling long sequences in the time domain for speech separation, a dual-path RNN was previously proposed by dividing lengthy sequences into shorter chunks and processing them with internal and external RNN components. Building upon this work, a Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN) model is presented here by integrating the dual-path RNN with Convolution Recurrent Networks. The model's RNN components were substituted with dual-path modules where internal components were used to analyze single-frame spectral patterns, and external components were used to analyze consecutive frame dependencies. Notably, with only 0.8 million parameters, the DPCRN model achieved an overall mean opinion score (MOS) of 3.57 in the wideband scenario of the Interspeech 2021 DNS challenge. Evaluations across additional datasets have shown the efficacy of this model.

Recently introduced multi-fluid models hold promise in refining the simulation of atmospheric convection within weather and climate simulations. A dynamic framework by nature, this method eliminates several of the mass-flux convection scheme's assumptions that are no longer valid at modern model resolution levels. Nonetheless, the optimal approach for solving the multi-fluid equations in relation to atmospheric convection remains unknown. The present paper outlines a simple single-column two-fluid model featuring ascending and descending fluid components with the exclusion of additional sub-filter variation modelling. Subsequent application to Rayleigh-Benard convection yields encouraging results as even a rudimentary model successfully replicates the prevalent characteristic overturning patterns of convection over a wide range of driving forces, accurately estimating the associated heat transfer scaling across six orders of magnitude.

We investigate three separate Jaynes-Cummings systems, with two of the systems having correlated atoms, but the third system is unconnected. Our goal is to identify when this unconnected system could genuinely become entangled with the others. Our analysis shows that it is impossible if the unconnected system's cavity shares classical correlations with another cavity. Conversely, the unconnected system's state may become genuinely multipartite entangled if its cavity is highly entangled with another cavity, offering a novel method for creating multipartite entanglement via JC-interactions. Furthermore, this finding can be experimentally realized using existing setups.

Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and manually annotated seven freely accessible Twitter sentiment
databases. We then compiled a new set of training and testing data from these sources. An
LSTM-based classification model was developed to determine the sentiment expressed in
individual tweets. The model's performance was assessed using the newly created dataset.

A nonlinear interaction occurs between electromagnetic fields in quantum electrodynamics, resulting in vacuum polarization. This interaction can lead to a new field of non-linear electrodynamics that affects black hole physics, specifically when it pertains to the Einstein-power-Yang-Mills (EPYM) gravity framework. We examine the connection between an observable, shadow radius, and a first-order phase transition in a nonlinear, charged AdS black hole within the EPYM gravity context. Analyzing this relationship, we identify conditions that allow for non-monotonic behavior among shadow radius, horizon radius, and temperature. Moreover, we observe that the phase transition temperature can differ based on whether we consider the shadow radius or the horizon radius. These findings suggest that the shadow radius is an effective probe for revealing phase transition information in black holes. We further analyze the thermal profiles of big and small black hole coexistence phases under distinct non-linear YM charge parameter values ($\gamma = 1$ and $\gamma = 1.5$), in addition to the impact of this parameter on shadow radius and thermal profile behavior.

Reconstructing a quantum state of continuous-variable systems like the radiation field is complicated, mainly due to the high dimensionality of its Hilbert space. Multiple approaches have been proposed for state reconstruction, including conventional methods and machine learning applications, yet there's no universally effective protocol for deriving the Wigner function from an optical tomogram of an arbitrary light state. We demonstrate that specific non-classical effects such as the generation of entanglement and onset of quantum synchronization are directly reflected in distinct patterns of optical tomograms, eliminating the need for full state reconstruction in these instances.

360-degree streaming videos offer engaging and immersive experiences but
require significant bandwidth. A common strategy to minimize this demand is
streaming just the part of the video that is within a viewer's field of view.
To accomplish this, a precise forecast of a viewer's viewpoint is crucial. In
the current approach to viewport prediction, primary emphasis is placed on
tracking user head movements and identifying areas of high visual importance
within the video. Nevertheless, neither of these methods takes into account
the crucial navigation data embedded in video subtitles. Such data, particularly
found in 360-degree virtual tourism videos, can significantly steer user
attention toward certain parts of the video. Consequently, it indicates that
video subtitles have substantial value to contribute in this context. Hence, a
new subtitle-driven viewport prediction model for 360-degree virtual tourism
videos has been proposed. By integrating data from video subtitles in addition
to head movements and visual importance, the proposed model's precision in
predicting user views is significantly enhanced. Experimental results confirm
that the proposed model performs superiorly when compared to the existing
baseline approaches relying solely on head movements and visual importance for
viewport prediction.

Tensor network methods have commonly been utilized in modeling different types of equilibrium and non-equilibrium situations. However, these techniques faced a critical challenge as their algorithms generally necessitated a small bond dimension at sufficiently low temperatures or time points, despite a fundamental requirement for approximating thermal states and time-evolved systems where the bond dimension is directly related to system size. This issue was tackled by constructing a specific class of objects that are able to accurately represent the thermal expectation values and time-evolved behavior for local observables in any scenario, where the bond dimension is completely independent of the system's size and is only determined by the temperature or elapsed time.
